source_metadata.exact_title: Initial management of intermediate- and high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: The review focuses on acute management of intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism (AHA C3, D1, D2) and high-risk pulmonary embolism (AHA E1, E2), emphasizing risk stratification and advanced therapies after CT-confirmed diagnosis.

The authors searched PubMed from 1980 through 2025 for pulmonary embolism terms combined with diagnosis, management, and treatment terms, manually searched relevant reference lists, and emphasized evidence from the preceding 15 years.

source_anchor.paragraph: Box 1: Evidence used in this review

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports an annual pulmonary embolism incidence of about 1 in 1000 in Canada, affecting more than 46,000 people and causing about one death every 8 hours.

population.label: People with pulmonary embolism in Canada

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that 9%–11% of patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism die within 30 days, with PE-related death in 2% and bleeding-related death in 0.5%.

population.label: Patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Among pulmonary embolism survivors, the review reports chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension in as many as 1%, chronic exertional breathlessness in almost 50%, and reduced quality of life in as many as half.

population.label: Survivors of pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Right ventricular dysfunction is presented as the main determinant of morbidity and death in acute pulmonary embolism because pulmonary arterial obstruction can raise RV afterload, leading to RV dilation, ischemia, systolic dysfunction, impaired LV filling, and low cardiac output.

source_anchor.paragraph: Why is risk stratification important for PE?

atoms.canonical_statement: High-risk pulmonary embolism is defined by hemodynamic instability, including systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg, vasopressor use, a persistent systolic pressure drop greater than 40 mm Hg from baseline, or cardiac arrest.

source_anchor.paragraph: How are intermediate–high-risk and high-risk PE defined and classified?

atoms.canonical_statement: Intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism is defined by systolic blood pressure above 90 mm Hg with right ventricular dysfunction; intermediate–low risk has either RV dysfunction or elevated cardiac biomarkers, whereas intermediate–high risk has both.

source_anchor.paragraph: How are intermediate–high-risk and high-risk PE defined and classified?

atoms.canonical_statement: Large database registries summarized in the review place high-risk pulmonary embolism at about 5%–10% of cases with in-hospital mortality of 15%–50%; cardiac-arrest presentations have mortality of 65%–90%.

population.label: Patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports short-term mortality of 5%–15% for intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism, a category comprising approximately 35%–55% of pulmonary embolism cases.

population.label: Patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Right ventricular dysfunction in pulmonary embolism is assessed with CT or echocardiography and cardiac-injury biomarkers such as troponin, BNP, or NT-proBNP; an RV-to-LV ratio of at least 1.0 is one imaging criterion.
Box 2 lists CT signs of RV dysfunction as RV-to-LV ratio at least 1.0, septal bowing or flattening toward the LV, and IV contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins.

source_anchor.paragraph: Box 2: Diagnostic criteria for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Box 2 lists echocardiographic signs of RV dysfunction as RV-to-LV ratio at least 1.0, septal bowing or flattening toward the LV, RV mid-cavitary diameter at least 35 mm, TAPSE at most 16 mm, McConnell sign, and tricuspid annular peak systolic velocity at most 9.5 cm/s.

source_anchor.paragraph: Box 2: Diagnostic criteria for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: The review cautions that RV dysfunction and troponin values behave as continuous risk factors, so binary normal/abnormal cutoffs can oversimplify graded risk.
PESI, simplified PESI, and Bova scores have only moderate discrimination for identifying patients who will deteriorate into high-risk pulmonary embolism.
Intermediate-risk patients can have impaired end-organ perfusion despite normal blood pressure, so systolic blood pressure alone may fail to identify normotensive cardiogenic shock.

source_anchor.paragraph: Beyond risk stratification, what clinical features are important to guide management?

atoms.canonical_statement: In an observational study summarized by the review, 34% of intermediate-risk patients with impaired end-organ perfusion despite normal blood pressure had an invasive cardiac index of 2.2 L/min/m² or less, meeting criteria for normotensive cardiogenic shock.

source_anchor.paragraph: Beyond risk stratification, what clinical features are important to guide management?

population.label: Intermediate-risk PE with impaired end-organ perfusion despite normal blood pressure

concept.text: Intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism with impaired end-organ perfusion

atoms.canonical_statement: Among patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism, serum lactate of at least 2 mmol/L was associated with 30-day mortality of 16.4% versus 1.6% in those with normal lactate.

source_anchor.paragraph: Beyond risk stratification, what clinical features are important to guide management?

population.label: Patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Hypoxemia and elevated respiratory rate are described as high-risk features in acute pulmonary embolism, and the 2026 AHA framework includes a respiratory modifier.

source_anchor.paragraph: Beyond risk stratification, what clinical features are important to guide management?

atoms.canonical_statement: The Composite PE Shock score uses six features: moderate or severe RV dysfunction, elevated troponin, elevated BNP, heart rate above 100 beats/min, central clot burden in a main pulmonary artery, and concomitant deep vein thrombosis.

In validation of the Composite PE Shock score, no patients with one or two features had normotensive shock, whereas three or more features were associated with normotensive cardiogenic shock and risk increased with each additional feature.

Point-of-care ultrasonography thresholds cited for identifying normotensive cardiogenic shock are RV outflow tract velocity-time integral of 9.5 cm/s or less and LV outflow tract velocity-time integral of 15 cm/s or less.

Because clinical features can change over hours to days, the review recommends serial assessment of clinical and laboratory parameters such as lactate and oxygen requirements to detect deterioration despite therapeutic anticoagulation.

Box 3 identifies persistent tachycardia above 110 beats/min, systolic blood pressure 90–100 mm Hg, shock index above 1, large central clot burden, escalating oxygen needs, syncope or presyncope, low-output signs, and lactate above 2 mmol/L as features associated with deterioration or death in intermediate–high-risk PE.

source_anchor.paragraph: Box 3: Clinical and laboratory features associated with elevated risk

atoms.canonical_statement: All patients with intermediate–high-risk or high-risk pulmonary embolism should receive immediate parenteral anticoagulation unless severe active bleeding contraindicates treatment.
Parenteral anticoagulation is preferred over oral anticoagulation during the first 48 hours of hospital admission for intermediate–high-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism.

The review states that ESC and AHA guidance prefer low-molecular-weight heparin over unfractionated heparin for initial parenteral anticoagulation in intermediate-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism.
Dalteparin dosing listed for intermediate–high-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism is 200 U/kg subcutaneously every 24 hours or 100 U/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours.

exposures.details: 200 U/kg every 24 h or 100 U/kg every 12 h

atoms.canonical_statement: Tinzaparin dosing listed for intermediate–high-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism is 175 U/kg subcutaneously every 24 hours or 88 U/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours.

exposures.details: 175 U/kg every 24 h or 88 U/kg every 12 h

atoms.canonical_statement: Enoxaparin dosing listed for intermediate–high-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours.
Unfractionated heparin dosing listed for intermediate–high-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism is an 80 U/kg IV bolus, maximum 5000 U, followed by an IV infusion of 18 U/kg/h.

exposures.details: 80 U/kg IV bolus (maximum 5000 U), then 18 U/kg/h IV infusion

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 identifies unfractionated heparin as the anticoagulant of preference when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min.
Alteplase dosing listed for systemic thrombolysis in pulmonary embolism includes 100 mg IV over 2 hours.

An alternative alteplase regimen listed for systemic thrombolysis is 0.6 mg/kg IV, maximum 50 mg, over 15 minutes; the review notes this may be considered for low body weight or elevated bleeding risk.

Tenecteplase dosing listed for systemic thrombolysis is weight based: 30 mg for <60 kg, 35 mg for 60–70 kg, 40 mg for 70–80 kg, 45 mg for 80–90 kg, and 50 mg for >90 kg, administered by IV push over 5–10 seconds.

exposures.details: <60 kg 30 mg; 60–70 kg 35 mg; 70–80 kg 40 mg; 80–90 kg 45 mg; >90 kg 50 mg; IV push over 5–10 s

atoms.canonical_statement: In a 505-patient observational study of pulmonary embolism treated with unfractionated heparin, fewer than half achieved therapeutic anticoagulation during the first 48 hours, and every patient had at least one supra- or subtherapeutic aPTT value.

population.label: Patients with pulmonary embolism receiving unfractionated heparin

concept.text: Achievement of therapeutic anticoagulation within 48 hours

atoms.canonical_statement: A retrospective study summarized in the review found enoxaparin use associated with lower mortality than unfractionated heparin in intermediate-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism.

population.label: Patients with intermediate-risk or high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: A 2017 Cochrane review of 29 randomized trials involving 10,390 patients with acute venous thromboembolism found fixed-dose LMWH associated with lower 3-month VTE recurrence, reduced thrombus size, and lower major hemorrhage rates than adjusted-dose unfractionated heparin.

population.label: Patients with acute venous thromboembolism in 29 randomized trials

concept.text: VTE recurrence, thrombus size, and major hemorrhage

atoms.canonical_statement: An audit of 1,045 US hospitals and 299,016 pulmonary embolism cases found unfractionated heparin use increased from 40% to 60% between 2011 and 2020 despite guideline preference for LMWH.

population.label: Pulmonary embolism cases in 1,045 US hospitals

concept.text: Use of unfractionated heparin over time

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism should receive ICU care; patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism should be considered for inpatient observation for deterioration, particularly when additional high-risk features are present.
For high-risk pulmonary embolism at a hospital without ICU services, the review advises considering interfacility transfer and weighing initiation of reperfusion therapy before transport.

The review describes pulmonary embolism response teams as a mechanism for real-time multidisciplinary recommendations and regional support, and notes 2026 AHA guidance recommending PERT referral for AHA categories C through E.
All patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism should be considered for advanced reperfusion therapy in addition to anticoagulation.
Retrospective data from Europe and the United States summarized in the review consistently indicate that fewer than half of patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism receive reperfusion therapy.

population.label: Patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Most patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism require no treatment beyond high-quality anticoagulation, but a subset with additional high-risk features, including AHA category D2, may be considered for advanced reperfusion therapy.

Advanced pulmonary embolism therapies described in the review include systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, and, in exceptional circumstances, surgical embolectomy.
The ESC and AHA guidelines summarized by the review recommend systemic thrombolysis as first-line advanced therapy for high-risk pulmonary embolism.

For high-risk pulmonary embolism, the review states that systemic thrombolysis plus anticoagulation reduces mortality compared with anticoagulation alone, although severe bleeding including intracranial hemorrhage is increased.

population.label: Patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: Evidence for systemic thrombolysis in high-risk pulmonary embolism is limited by a small randomized evidence base of approximately 224 high-risk patients and absence of placebo-controlled randomized trials since 1995.
No study has directly compared alteplase with tenecteplase in pulmonary embolism, and the ideal thrombolytic agent and dosing regimen for high-risk pulmonary embolism remain uncertain.

In the PEITHO trial of 1,005 intermediate–high-risk patients, tenecteplase plus standard anticoagulation reduced the composite of hemodynamic decompensation or death versus placebo plus anticoagulation, but increased extracranial bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage; the composite benefit was driven mainly by less hemodynamic decompensation without a significant mortality reduction.

population.label: Patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism in PEITHO

concept.text: Hemodynamic decompensation or death and major bleeding

atoms.canonical_statement: At 6-month follow-up after PEITHO, markers of right ventricular dysfunction were not different between thrombolysis and placebo groups.

population.label: PEITHO trial participants

atoms.canonical_statement: Routine full-dose systemic thrombolysis is not recommended for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism; the review notes that AHA guidance allows consideration of systemic thrombolysis for incipient cardiopulmonary failure (category D).
A randomized trial is investigating reduced-dose systemic thrombolysis in a subset of intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism patients to improve reperfusion while reducing bleeding risk.

Box 4 lists absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis including prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 6 months, brain or spine surgery within 3 months, serious head trauma within 3 months, severe active bleeding, and CNS neoplasm.

Box 4 lists relative contraindications to systemic thrombolysis including recent major trauma or surgery, coagulopathy, therapeutic oral anticoagulation or dual antiplatelet therapy, severe hypertension, recent TIA, age at least 75 years, structural CNS abnormality or GI neoplasm, late pregnancy or early postpartum status, traumatic CPR, noncompressible-site bleeding, and advanced liver disease.

Catheter-based interventions are recommended for high-risk pulmonary embolism when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated, and should also be considered when high-risk patients fail to improve after systemic thrombolysis.
The review notes that AHA guidance considers catheter-based therapy an option for intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism with incipient cardiopulmonary failure and for cardiogenic shock.

A network meta-analysis summarized in the review suggested catheter-directed thrombolysis may reduce mortality and bleeding compared with systemic thrombolysis, but high-risk-specific comparisons were uncommon and randomized direct evidence was sparse.

population.label: Patients with intermediate- or high-risk pulmonary embolism in a network meta-analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: In the FLAME observational registry summarized by the review, first-line mechanical thrombectomy for high-risk pulmonary embolism had reported in-hospital mortality of 1.9%.

population.label: High-risk pulmonary embolism patients undergoing first-line mechanical thrombectomy

atoms.canonical_statement: The review cautions that the 1.9% in-hospital mortality reported in the FLAME registry is dramatically lower than historical registry rates and should be interpreted cautiously until randomized evidence is available.

For intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism, timing and patient selection for catheter-based therapy remain incompletely defined; apparent benefit from earlier treatment may partly reflect differences in natural clinical trajectory.

In an international randomized trial of selected intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed fibrinolysis plus anticoagulation reduced the 7-day composite of cardiorespiratory decompensation, death, or PE recurrence to 4.0% versus 10.3% with anticoagulation alone.

population.label: Intermediate–high-risk PE with at least two additional high-risk clinical features

concept.text: Cardiorespiratory decompensation, death, or PE recurrence

atoms.canonical_statement: In that catheter-directed fibrinolysis trial, the composite benefit was driven primarily by reduced hemodynamic decompensation; mortality, PE recurrence, and major bleeding were not significantly different between groups.

population.label: Intermediate–high-risk PE with at least two additional high-risk clinical features

concept.text: Mortality, PE recurrence, major bleeding, and hemodynamic decompensation

atoms.canonical_statement: In a randomized trial comparing mechanical thrombectomy with catheter-directed thrombolysis for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism, 95% of participants were intermediate–high risk and clinical deterioration occurred in 1.5% versus 3.6%, respectively.

source_anchor.paragraph: Mechanical thrombectomy versus catheter-directed thrombolysis RCT paragraph

population.label: Intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism trial population; 95% intermediate–high risk

atoms.canonical_statement: In a randomized trial of 100 intermediate–high-risk patients, mechanical thrombectomy plus anticoagulation produced greater reduction in RV-to-LV ratio and more frequent normalization of vital signs than anticoagulation alone, without a significant difference in major adverse events.

source_anchor.paragraph: Mechanical thrombectomy plus anticoagulation RCT paragraph

population.label: Patients with intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism

concept.text: RV-to-LV ratio, vital-sign normalization, and major adverse events

atoms.canonical_statement: The review concludes that additional high-quality randomized trials comparing catheter-based therapy plus anticoagulation with anticoagulation alone are needed to define the role of advanced interventions in intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism.

ECMO is described as mechanical circulatory support for extreme high-risk pulmonary embolism with impending or established cardiovascular collapse, including possible deployment during cardiac arrest.
The evidence for ECMO in high-risk pulmonary embolism is conflicting across retrospective studies, and bleeding, ischemic, and infectious complications are common.

Retrospective evidence summarized in the review suggests systemic thrombolysis before or during ECMO improves the odds of survival to hospital discharge without substantial increases in bleeding compared with ECMO alone.

population.label: High-risk pulmonary embolism patients receiving ECMO

concept.text: Systemic thrombolysis before or during ECMO
Survival to hospital discharge and bleeding

atoms.canonical_statement: If ECMO is being considered for high-risk pulmonary embolism, the review strongly advises early discussion and logistical planning with quaternary referral centres.
A clot-in-transit is defined as image-detected embolization of thrombus before it reaches the pulmonary arteries, usually visualized in the right heart chambers on echocardiography or CT.

source_anchor.paragraph: How should a clot-in-transit be managed?

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports clot-in-transit in as many as 8%–9% of patients with pulmonary embolism and associates its presence with higher mortality.

source_anchor.paragraph: How should a clot-in-transit be managed?

population.label: Patients with pulmonary embolism

atoms.canonical_statement: There is no consensus management strategy for clot-in-transit; options described include anticoagulation alone, systemic thrombolysis, catheter-based therapy, and surgical embolectomy.

source_anchor.paragraph: How should a clot-in-transit be managed?

atoms.canonical_statement: For clot-in-transit, the review states that systemic thrombolysis or catheter-based therapy may be associated with lower mortality than other approaches.

source_anchor.paragraph: How should a clot-in-transit be managed?

population.label: Patients with pulmonary embolism and clot-in-transit

atoms.canonical_statement: When a thrombus straddles a patent foramen ovale and threatens systemic embolization, surgical embolectomy with patent foramen ovale closure may be considered.

source_anchor.paragraph: How should a clot-in-transit be managed?

atoms.canonical_statement: The review concludes that management of intermediate–high-risk and high-risk pulmonary embolism begins with prompt anticoagulation and risk stratification, while hemodynamic instability, shock, or cardiac arrest can warrant immediate advanced therapy.
Intermediate–high-risk pulmonary embolism should be repeatedly reassessed for worsening perfusion, and catheter-based interventions are increasingly used in selected patients.

The review identifies equitable access to advanced pulmonary embolism therapies and PERT consultation across Canada as priorities for improving outcomes and reducing geographic and health-system disparities.

The review identifies unresolved questions about barriers to appropriate anticoagulation and advanced therapy use, which intermediate–high-risk subgroup should receive advanced therapy and which modality, and whether catheter-based therapy can serve as first-line treatment for high-risk pulmonary embolism.

extraction_limitations: The governing LiteratureAtom model is explicitly oriented to primary literature, whereas this source is a narrative review.

Quantitative and comparative findings originating in cited studies are represented only as secondary reports from this review, anchored to the review page and tagged secondary_reported_result; they are not primary-study extractions.

Where the review supplied direction or ranges without a point estimate compatible with the QuantitativeResult contract, the claim was retained as a qualitative_result rather than fabricating an estimate.
The bibliography was not atomized; reference entries were treated as provenance infrastructure rather than independent evidence assertions.
The schema has no dedicated recommendation/guideline-synthesis atom kind, so review recommendations were mapped primarily to author_conclusion and tagged to preserve their role.
This extraction does not independently verify the cited primary studies or current guideline text.
schema_gaps: No first-class source-type field distinguishes primary-study atoms from secondary-source synthesis.
No dedicated atom kind for guideline/review recommendations or evidence-synthesis statements.
QuantitativeResult requires a point estimate, which is not ideal for source-reported ranges or threshold-only comparative statements.
